newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France wants new Cr Lyonnais bailout plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France wants new Cr Lyonnais bailout plan.

text.p: France has told the European Commission it wants to revise a bailout of Credit Lyonnais last year which threatens to plunge the state-controlled bank back into loss, a senior French source said on Tuesday.

But officials at the European Commission, which gave the green light to the massive 1995 aid package, said there was outrage at the possibility of more state help and warned that the Commission would attach tough conditions to any approval.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert was due to give a news conference on Wednesday on the bank, whose near downfall after a runaway expansion in the late 1980s marked the biggest banking scandal in recent French history.
The French finance ministry refused to comment and the Commission in Brussels did not elaborate.

But Credit Lyonnais, bailed out by the state in 1994 and again in 1995, announced without further clarification that it had postponed the release of its first-half results to October 3 from this Thursday.
One French source said this was to give the Commission time to consider the finance ministry's request on new rescue terms.

The government had notified Brussels that it wanted to renegotiate the interest rate charged on a 119 billion franc ($23.22 billion) loan granted by Credit Lyonnais to a state rescue vehicle that took over 130 billion francs of its troubled assets last year, the source said.

In 1995, the Commission agreed to a multiannual rescue plan involving a maximum subsidy of 45 billion francs on the condition that the bank share part of its restructuring costs, sold 35 percent of its foreign assets and was privatised.

In particular, the Commission insisted on the low interest loan to the rescue defeasance vehicle known as the the Public Body for Financing and Restructuring (EPFR) that took over the bank's problem assets.

But the bank has said the shortfall on the loan will cost it three billion francs this year. This, banking analysts, have said could push the bank into a loss of several billion francs in 1995 after it crawled back into profit in 1995.

The government and Credit Lyonnais have been negotiating for months on new rescue terms. Sources have said with the burden of the loan lifted, the bank might be able to post a small profit for the first half.
The bank accumulated 21 billion francs of losses between 1992 and 1994 before eking out a 13 million franc profit in 1995.
Under the 1995 rescue approved by the Commission, the bank must sell at least 35 percent of its foreign assets, including a substantial part of its European banking network by the end of 1998.

In exchange for approving new rescue terms, the European Commission could demand that it sell additional assets, in particular the bank's profitable German unit Bank Fuer Gemeinwirtschaft. But Credit Lyonnais has already said it is reluctant to sell that asset.
Press reports have said the total cost of the bank's expansion spree to French taxpayers could eventually hit 100 billion francs. ($1=5.124 French Franc)
